recipe.history:
Foie gras — the fatted liver of a duck or goose — is one of the most luxurious and contested ingredients in the culinary world, with a history stretching back to ancient Egypt, where wall paintings at Saqqara dating to 2500 BCE depict workers force-feeding geese with figs. The Romans adopted the practice enthusiastically, calling the resulting liver ficatum — from ficus, fig, the feed used — which is the etymological root of the modern words for liver in French (foie), Spanish (hígado), and Italian (fegato). It was the French, however, who refined gavage into a high art, particularly in the Périgord and Alsace regions, where duck and goose foie gras became emblematic of the finest French cooking. The truffle, foie gras's frequent companion, shares a similarly ancient Mediterranean history — prized by Sumerians, celebrated by the Romans as the food of the gods, and perfected by French chefs who learned that the combination of earthy fungus and unctuous liver was among the most compelling in all of gastronomy.

The arrival of foie gras and truffle on the American burger was an inevitable consequence of the gastropub movement of the 2000s, when chefs who had trained in classical kitchens began operating casual burger counters where they could apply haute cuisine techniques and ingredients to a plebeian format. Daniel Boulud's DB Burger at DB Bistro Moderne in New York — a sirloin patty stuffed with braised short rib and filled with foie gras and black truffle — appeared in 2001 and became one of the most famous (and at the time, most expensive) burgers in America. It legitimized the concept of the luxury burger and opened the door to truffle fries on the burger itself, foie gras butter melting over a crust, aged cheddar chosen for complexity rather than convenience. The "cheat day" burger was born: the sandwich you eat when you've abandoned all restraint.

There is a particular kind of meal you eat when you've decided that today, just today, none of the ordinary rules apply. The last time I made this burger I had been traveling for two weeks on an assignment that left me eating sad hotel food and room service sandwiches, and when I finally got home I pulled everything extravagant I had out of the refrigerator and the pantry. I made the fries thick and twice-fried until crackling, shaved truffle over them while they were still hot, and set the whole pile on a double-stacked patty with a knob of foie gras butter melting into the crust and aged cheddar collapsing over the edges. The brioche bun was slathered with Dijon aioli. It took forty-five minutes to make and about six minutes to eat and I thought about it for the rest of the week.

On a burger of this ambition and richness, cooking the patty to medium rare is not a luxury — it is a structural requirement. A well-done patty would be a dry, dense puck under the weight of foie gras butter, truffle fries, and aged cheddar; the fat would have left the meat and the whole composition would collapse into greasy chaos. At 130–135°F, the patty is still juicy enough to hold its own against every extravagant element piled on top of it. The medium rare center — pink, yielding, silky — is the axis around which this indulgence turns. Every other ingredient exists to amplify the experience of good beef cooked correctly. Cut corners here and you have only expensive ingredients on a mediocre sandwich.
ingredients: 180g (¾ cup) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream (egg wash)
115g (4 oz) grade A duck foie gras, deveined and at room temperature
1 liter (4 cups) peanut or canola oil for frying
1 tbsp fresh flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
1–2 tsp black truffle shavings or 1 tsp truffle salt (optional but ideal)
170g (6 oz) aged cheddar (2-year minimum), sliced thick
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl. Mix on low with dough hook.
2. Add eggs and warm milk. Mix until a rough dough forms, about 3 minutes on low.
3. Knead on medium speed for 8 minutes until smooth. Add butter a few cubes at a time with the mixer running, waiting until each addition is fully absorbed. This takes 8–10 minutes.
4. Knead 5 more minutes until dough is silky and pulls away from the bowl. Cover and refrigerate overnight.
5. Next day, divide into 4 portions, shape into balls, place on a lined sheet pan, flatten slightly. Proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 18–20 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a rack.
7. MAKE THE FOIE GRAS BUTTER — Sear the foie gras in a very hot dry skillet for 30 seconds per side until browned. Do not overcook — it should still be soft inside. Let cool slightly.
8. Blend the seared foie gras in a food processor until smooth. Add softened butter, Cognac, thyme, fleur de sel, and white pepper. Pulse until fully combined and smooth.
9. Scrape onto plastic wrap, roll into a log, and refrigerate until firm, at least 1 hour. Slice into rounds when ready to use.
10. MAKE THE TRUFFLE FRIES — Cut potatoes into ¼-inch sticks. Soak in cold water 30 minutes, then drain and dry completely on kitchen towels.
11. Heat oil to 325°F (163°C) in a heavy pot. Fry potatoes in batches for 4–5 minutes until cooked through but not yet browned. Remove and drain on a wire rack. Let cool completely.
12. Increase oil temperature to 375°F (190°C). Fry the blanched potatoes again in batches for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Drain immediately.
13. While fries are still hot, toss in a bowl with truffle oil, parsley, truffle shavings or truffle salt, and fleur de sel. Set aside — they will go on the burger.

14. FORM THE PATTIES — Divide beef into 8 equal portions (about 115g / 4 oz each). Form into thin patties about ½-inch thick. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
15. MAKE THE DIJON AIOLI — Stir together mayonnaise, Dijon, grated garlic, and lemon juice until smooth. Set aside.
16. COOK THE PATTIES — Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat with a thin film of neutral oil until smoking.
17. Cook 4 patties at a time undisturbed for 2 minutes. Flip. Lay 1 slice of aged cheddar on each patty. Cook 1½–2 more minutes.
18. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Because these are thinner patties, cooking time is shorter — watch carefully.
19. Remove first batch and repeat with remaining 4 patties.
20. Immediately place a round of foie gras butter on top of each hot patty and let it melt into the crust.
21. Stack two patties per burger (foie gras butter side facing each other or up — your call).
22. Rest under foil 2 minutes.
23. TOAST THE BUNS — Split brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat until golden, 60 seconds.
24. ASSEMBLE — Spread Dijon aioli on both cut sides of each bun.
25. Place the double patty stack on the bottom bun.
26. Pile a generous handful of truffle fries directly on top of the patties.
27. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately before the fries have time to second-guess the situation.
